design_detail: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42023462484) with random-effects meta-analyses of standardized mean differences for polysomnographic or EEG sleep measures (total sleep time, sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, N1, N2, slow-wave sleep, REM sleep, REM latency) in studies of cannabis or cannabinoid administration, chronic use against no use, and withdrawal. 18 studies included (1972-1982 and 2004 onward); 9 entered meta-analyses: 6 of administration (all oral products: THC, dronabinol, CBD or combinations) and 3 of withdrawal.
can_establish: What sleep-laboratory studies have found, on average, for sleep measured during use of oral cannabis products (mostly modern trials of CBD or low-dose THC, mostly in people with sleep disorders), and for sleep in the first days after people stop regular cannabis use or daily high-dose THC.
cannot_establish: Effects of smoked or vaped cannabis on sleep architecture (no eligible modern study), effects of the doses and products most people use, effects in people who use cannabis daily while they continue, how long withdrawal sleep problems last beyond the first week, or effects on how rested people feel (subjective sleep was outside the review).

sample.recruitment: Embase, Medline and Web of Science searched on 2 September 2023 without restrictions; screening in Covidence by two reviewers with two others resolving conflicts (pp. 3, 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Any form of cannabis (THC, CBD, nabilone, dronabinol, whole plant); sleep measured by EEG, polysomnography, polygraphy or actigraphy; at least one of nine sleep outcomes; a comparison (pre-post or control group). Excluded: cannabis only as a moderator, cannabis combined with other substances without isolating its effect, and non-English publications (p. 5).
sample.demographics: Early studies (1972-1982): samples of 2 to 11 (mean 5.6), all young adult men aged 21-29, healthy, given THC at doses up to far above modern trials (exposure field). Modern studies: 8 to 73 participants (mean 29.7), mean age 49.8, 55.5% men, four of six in sleep disorders (obstructive sleep apnea, insomnia, REM behaviour disorder in Parkinson's disease) (pp. 6-7; Table 1, p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: English only; three databases, no grey literature or registries; all early administration studies lacked the statistics needed for pooling, so the administration meta-analyses contain only modern trials of oral medicinal products, while two of the three withdrawal studies pooled are early high-dose studies (p. 9).

exposure.measurement: Cannabis or cannabinoid given by investigators (administration and early withdrawal studies) or self-reported use (comparisons of people who use cannabis with people who do not, and real-world withdrawal studies); purity of plant material not commonly reported (p. 13).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Table 1, p. 4; pp. 6, 11-12): pooled administration trials used oral THC and THC:CBD combinations (15:0, 5:5 and 15:15 mg), dronabinol titrated 2.5-10 mg, CBD 300 mg or titrated 75-300 mg, and a THC:CBN:CBD 10:1:0.5 mg product, over 4 to 84 days; early studies used oral THC up to 70-210 mg a day or 0.2-1.4 mg/kg. Withdrawal studies pooled: two early studies stopping 70-210 mg a day of oral THC in men with a history of daily use (n = 7 and 11) and one modern study of 20 people actively using cannabis who stopped (inhaled, real-world use).
exposure.polysubstance: Studies combining cannabis with other substances without isolating its effect were excluded; other drug use in the comparison and withdrawal samples is not summarized.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Administration studies: washouts of two weeks to two months in six, self-reported abstinence in two, urine confirmation in three; withdrawal data taken from the first three days in two studies and days four to six in one (pp. 8-9).

comparison.controls: Placebo (crossover or parallel), pre-post baselines, or non-using comparison groups, depending on the study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep disorders in most modern samples; prior cannabis use unspecified in two administration studies; in withdrawal, sleep before regular use began is unknown.

outcomes.instruments: Polysomnography or EEG in every included study; one study also used actigraphy, but its polysomnography data were pooled (p. 7).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard sleep staging; no subjective sleep outcomes.
outcomes.operationalization: Standardized mean differences between cannabis and comparison conditions for each sleep measure.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; risk of bias in primary studies rated with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I (Tables 2 and 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Administration, SMD (95% CI) as printed in the forest plots: total sleep time -0.02 (-0.25 to 0.21), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency -0.06 (-0.28 to 0.17), 0%; wake after sleep onset 0.11 (-0.13 to 0.34), 0%; sleep efficiency 0.01 (-0.25 to 0.27), 0%; N1 0.15 (-0.07 to 0.37); N2 0.01 (-0.21 to 0.23); slow-wave sleep 0.14 (-0.07 to 0.35); REM -0.04 (-0.52 to 0.45), I-squared 77.5%; REM latency -0.03 (-0.56 to 0.50), I-squared 76.1% (Figs. 2-10, pp. 6-11). Withdrawal: total sleep time -0.79 (-1.16 to -0.42), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency 1.21 (0.76 to 1.67), 6.4%; sleep efficiency -0.92 (-1.38 to -0.46), 0% (two studies); REM 1.61 (0.74 to 2.48), 46.8%; REM latency -1.09 (-1.53 to -0.66), 0%.
analysis.covariates: None; sensitivity analyses removing two studies without prior-use information and two CBD-only studies did not change significance (p. 11).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42023462484 (p. 3). Funnel plots and Egger tests were planned but not done because of the small number of studies (pp. 6, 9); a sensitivity analysis excluding high risk-of-bias studies was planned (p. 6) and its results are not reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Text and figures disagree on the sign of four administration estimates (see reporting issues); the planned risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis is not reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed; the authors stress the thin evidence base (six administration and three withdrawal studies in meta-analyses) (p. 12).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In six modern trials of oral cannabis products (mostly CBD or low-dose THC medicines, four of six in people with sleep disorders, 178 participants), no sleep measure differed on average from the comparison condition, with narrow intervals for sleep time, onset, waking and efficiency but wide, inconsistent results for REM sleep. In three withdrawal studies (about 38 people), sleep in the first week after stopping was shorter, slower to start and less efficient, with more and earlier REM sleep, by large standardized amounts; two of the three withdrew high experimental oral THC doses in the 1970s.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and practice points say cannabis administration does not consistently alter sleep architecture and that withdrawal from chronic use significantly disrupts sleep (pp. 1, 13); the conclusion advises clinicians not to view cannabis as a reliable sleep aid and to prepare people who use regularly for transient insomnia when quitting (p. 13). The administration statement is accurate for the pooled oral products and populations but is phrased for cannabis in general, which was not studied in its common inhaled form; the withdrawal statement rests on three small studies, two of them withdrawals of experimental high doses, though the authors call the estimates tiny-cohort and cautious (p. 13). The authors rated an uncontrolled pre-post withdrawal study as low risk of bias.

timeline.event: Angarita et al., narrative review of sleep in alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioid use, describing withdrawal sleep problems second-hand.
This review: by the authors' account the first meta-analysis of polysomnographic sleep architecture and cannabis.

replication.where_it_stands: The only quantitative synthesis of measured sleep architecture with cannabis identified by its authors. Its administration pools rest on modern oral medicinal trials and its withdrawal pools largely on 1970s high-dose studies plus one modern study (Vandrey et al., 2011), which narrative reviews such as Angarita et al. (2016) also cite, so the two are not independent.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 14).
funding.affiliations_note: First and last authors are affiliated with the clinical research department of Tranq Sleep Care, a sleep clinic in Kelowna, Canada, and with the University of British Columbia.

what_would_settle_it: Preregistered, adequately powered sleep-laboratory studies of inhaled cannabis at doses people use, in people who use it regularly and occasionally, including nights during use and repeated nights after stopping, with objective and subjective sleep measures and next-day functioning.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Cannabis exposures, comparisons (pre-post or control), polysomnographic outcomes and study types are specified.
Registered in PROSPERO; the registered content was not examined, and planned analyses (publication bias, risk-of-bias sensitivity) were not done or not reported.
Any design with a pre-post or control comparison was admitted without a stated reason for mixing randomized trials with uncontrolled designs.

Three databases without search restrictions, but non-English papers were excluded at eligibility without justification (three excluded for language), and no grey literature, registries or reference lists.
Two reviewers screened, with two others resolving conflicts.
Each charted study underwent double review (p. 6).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The flow diagram gives counts by reason only (supplement 41, outcome 15, method 6, review 4, language 3 and others); no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, blinding, control, duration, prior use, sex, age, condition, size, route, product, dose, direction of each outcome and risk of bias.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 for randomized and ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies, with domain-level judgments shown (Tables 2 and 3); the ROBINS-I ratings use a three-level scheme and rate an uncontrolled pre-post study low.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: A non-randomized uncontrolled study (Farabi et al., 2014) is pooled with randomized trials in four administration analyses; CBD and THC products and different patient groups are combined in single pools; the handling of crossover and pre-post correlations is not described beyond pooling means and SDs.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis excluding high risk-of-bias studies was planned, but no result is reported, although two of three withdrawal studies pooled were rated high risk.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion repeatedly weighs the early studies' methodological limits and calls the withdrawal estimates tiny-cohort and cautious.
I-squared reported; heterogeneity in REM measures examined in sensitivity analyses and discussed in terms of dose, product, tolerance and sleep apnea.
Planned but not done because of the small number of studies.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: More than one critical item is not met (restricted search, inappropriate pooling of randomized and non-randomized designs, no list of excluded studies, no publication-bias assessment), so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. The review is registered, transparent about its thin evidence base and careful in its discussion; its tables and forest plots allow each pooled result to be traced. It can be cited for what measured sleep looked like in the few pooled studies, with their populations and products named; not for effects of inhaled cannabis or for a precise size of withdrawal effects.

key_findings.finding: 18 studies included: 9 administration only, 2 chronic use only, 1 withdrawal only, 5 administration and withdrawal, 1 chronic use and withdrawal; 9 in meta-analyses (6 administration, 3 withdrawal). Studies came from 1972-1982 and from 2004 onward, none in between.

Administration, pooled SMD (95% CI): total sleep time -0.02 (-0.25 to 0.21), 5 arms from 4 studies; sleep onset latency -0.06 (-0.28 to 0.17), 6 arms from 5 studies; wake after sleep onset 0.11 (-0.13 to 0.34); sleep efficiency 0.01 (-0.25 to 0.27); all I-squared 0-6%. Of 12 administration studies measuring total sleep time, one (n = 4) found an increase and 11 no change; of 12 measuring onset latency, one (n = 2) found an increase.
key_findings.note: Signs as printed in the forest plots; the text prints +0.021, +0.056 and -0.009 for total sleep time, onset latency and efficiency (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Administration, sleep stages: N1 0.15 (-0.07 to 0.37); N2 0.01 (-0.21 to 0.23); slow-wave sleep 0.14 (-0.07 to 0.35); REM -0.04 (-0.52 to 0.45), I-squared 77.5% (dronabinol in sleep apnea raised REM, 1.16 and 0.72; CBD in REM behaviour disorder lowered it, -0.98); REM latency -0.03 (-0.56 to 0.50), I-squared 76.1%. Of 14 administration studies, six (mostly early high-dose THC studies of 4 to 11 people, and one CBD study) found less REM sleep and one more.

Withdrawal, pooled SMD (95% CI), three studies (Feinberg et al., 1975, n = 7; Feinberg et al., 1976, n = 11; Vandrey et al., 2011, n = 20): total sleep time -0.79 (-1.16 to -0.42); sleep onset latency 1.21 (0.76 to 1.67); REM sleep 1.61 (0.74 to 2.48), I-squared 46.8%; REM latency -1.09 (-1.53 to -0.66); sleep efficiency (two studies) -0.92 (-1.38 to -0.46). Individual studies all in the same direction (for example total sleep time -0.95, -0.89 and -0.70).
key_findings.locator: Figs. 2b, 3b, 5b, 9b and 10b (pp. 6-11); Results 3.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.4, 3.2.8 (pp. 10-11) and 3.2.9 (p. 12); Table 1 sample sizes (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Minus signs checked on the rendered forest plots.

key_findings.finding: Across all seven withdrawal studies: total sleep time fell in 3 and did not change in 4; time to fall asleep rose in 5 of 7; REM rose in 3 of 7; wake after sleep onset rose in 3 of 7. Withdrawal data came from the first three nights in the two early studies and nights four to six in the modern one.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1.5, last paragraphs (p. 9, right column); 3.2.1 to 3.2.3 (p. 10); 3.2.8 (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Two of the three withdrawal studies in the meta-analyses (Feinberg et al., 1975 and 1976) replaced high daily experimental doses of oral THC (exposure field) with placebo in men with a history of daily use; the third (Vandrey et al., 2011) compared sleep before and during abstinence in 20 people actively using cannabis, who knew they had stopped. ROBINS-I: the two early studies high risk overall, the modern study low.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 withdrawal rows (p. 4); Table 2 (p. 5); Results 3.1.2 (p. 8); Discussion (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Comparisons of people who use cannabis with people who do not (three studies with inhaled cannabis, 1973-2008): no significant differences in most measures; one found shorter total sleep time and less slow-wave sleep, one more REM.

Sensitivity analyses removing the two administration studies that did not specify prior use, and the two CBD-only studies, did not change the significance of any administration result or reduce REM heterogeneity.

Practice points: no consistent effect of administration on sleep parameters; REM suppression in high-dose 1970s trials and mixed findings in modern trials; withdrawal from chronic use reduces sleep time and lengthens sleep onset, though polysomnographic evidence is scarce.

reporting_issues.issue: Four administration estimates have a different sign in the text than in the forest plots: total sleep time +0.021 in the text against -0.02 in Fig. 2a; sleep onset latency +0.056 against -0.06 (Fig. 3a); sleep efficiency -0.009 against 0.01 (Fig. 5a); REM +0.0356 against -0.04 (Fig. 9a). In each case the text's confidence interval is centred on the figure's sign.
reporting_issues.consequence: The point estimates are near zero, so conclusions do not change, but the figures are the values to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls the administration REM latency result one with no heterogeneity while printing I-squared 76.12% (p. 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: Heterogeneity was high for REM latency as for REM.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says one study focused only on chronic use (p. 7), but the flow diagram and Table 1 show two (pp. 3-4); it says three withdrawal studies used pre-post measures, citing references 46-48 (p. 8), but reference 47 is not among the seven withdrawal studies in Table 1, so the stated design counts sum to eight.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 1 is the record to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 codes Vandrey et al. (2011) as double-blind, while the text says participants in the pre-post withdrawal studies were aware of cessation (p. 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: The modern withdrawal study is better read as an open pre-post comparison, which affects its low risk-of-bias rating.

reporting_issues.issue: The search is described as having no restrictions (p. 5), but non-English publications were excluded at eligibility (p. 5; three excluded for language in Fig. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: A language restriction applied in practice.
